source_text: Homilia in paralyticum juxta piscinam jacentem Τοῦ ἐν ἁγίοις πατρὸς ἡμῶν ΚΥΡΙΛΛΟΥ ἀρχιεπισκόπου Ἱεροσολύμων ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΠΑΡΑΛΥΤΙΚΟΝ τὸν ἐπὶ τὴν κολυμβήθραν. 1 Ὅπου ἂν φανῇ Ἰησοῦς, ἐκεῖ καὶ ἡ σωτηρία. κἄν τε γὰρ ἴδῃ τελώνην καθήμενον ἐπὶ τοῦ τελωνίου, τοῦτον ἀπόστολον ποιεῖ καὶ εὐαγγελιστήν, κἄν τε μετὰ νεκρῶν ταφῇ, νεκροὺς ἐγείρει. καὶ τυφλοῖς μὲν τὸ βλέπειν χαρίζεται, κωφοῖς δὲ τὸ ἀκούειν. καὶ τὰς κολυμβήθρας περιέρχεται, οὐ τὰς οἰκοδομὰς ζητῶν, ἀλλὰ τοὺς νοσοῦντας ἰατρεύων. 2 Ἐν γὰρ τοῖς Ἱεροσολύμοις ἦν προβατικὴ κολυμβήθρα πέντε στοὰς ἔχουσα, τέσσαρας μὲν περιτρεχούσας, μέσην δὲ τὴν πέμπτην, ἐν ᾗ κατέκειτο πλῆθος ἀσθενούντων. καὶ ἀπιστία ἦν πολλὴ τῶν Ἰουδαίων. ὁ δὲ τῶν ψυχῶν καὶ σωμάτων ἰατρὸς καὶ θεραπευτὴς μέτρῳ τὴν ἴασιν ἐχαρίζετο, τὸν πολυχρόνιον πρῶτον θεραπεύων, ἵνα τάχιον ἀπαλλαγῇ τῶν ἀλγηδόνων. οὐ γὰρ μία ἡμέρα ἦν αὐτῷ κατακεῖσθαι, ὡς οὐδὲ δευτέρα, οὐδὲ πρῶτος μὴν ἢ ἐνιαυτός, ἀλλ' ὀκτὼ καὶ τριάκοντα ἔτη. κατακείμενος πολυχρονίῳ νόσῳ γνώριμος ἦν τοῖς ὁρῶσιν, καὶ δεικνύων τοῦ θεραπεύοντος τὴν ἐνέργειαν. ἐγνωρίζετο γὰρ ὑπὸ πάντων διὰ τὸν χρόνον ὁ παραλυτικός. ὁ δὲ ἀρχιατρὸς ἐδείκνυ μὲν τὴν δύναμιν, ἠθετεῖτο δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν κακῶς ἐκδεχομένων. 3 Περιερχόμενος δὲ τὴν κολυμβήθραν ἴδεν, οὐκ ἐξ ἐρωτήσεως μαθών, ἀλλ' ἐκ θεϊκῆς ἐνεργείας τὸ λεῖπον ἀπεπλή ρωσεν. ἰδών, οὐκ ἐρωτῶν, ἐκ πόσου χρόνου κατάκειται, ἀλλ' ἰδὼν ἔγνω, ὁ καὶ πρὸ τοῦ ἰδεῖν εἰδώς. εἰ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ καρδίαν οὐ χρείαν εἶχεν ἵνα τις αὐτὸν ἐρωτήσῃ περὶ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (αὐτὸς γὰρ ᾔδει, τί ἦν ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ), πολὺ δὲ μᾶλλον περὶ τῶν νοσημάτων, ὧν ἔξωθεν ἡ ἐπαγωγή. 4 Εἶδεν τινὰ κατακείμενον καὶ πλείστῃ νόσῳ βεβαρημένον. ἁμαρτιῶν γὰρ εἶχε πολὺ φορτίον καὶ νόσου πολυχρόνιον ἀλγηδόνα. πρὸς τοῦτον ἐρώτημά πως λέγει τὸ ποθούμενον· θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι; καὶ οὐκ εἶπεν τὶ ἄλλο, ἀλλὰ κατέλειπεν τῇ μεσότητι τῆς ἐρωτήσεως. διπλῆ γὰρ ἦν ἡ ἐρώτησις. ἐπειδὴ γὰρ οὐ μόνον ἐνόσει τὸ σῶμα, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν ψυχήν, (κατὰ τὸ ὕστερον ὑπ' αὐτοῦ εἰρημένον, ἴδε ὑγιὴς γέγονας, μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε, ἵνα μὴ χεῖρόν σοί τι γένηται,) ἠρώτα αὐτόν· θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι; ὢ μεγάλης ἰατροῦ δυνάμεως, ἐπὶ τῷ θέλειν τὴν βοήθειαν τιθεμένου. ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἐκ πίστεως ἡ σωτηρία, διὰ τοῦτο ἤκουσε τὸ θέλεις, ἵνα τὸ θέλειν ἐπαγάγῃ τὴν ἐνέργειαν. τοῦτο μόνου τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τὸ ῥῆμα. ἀρχιάτρων γὰρ οὐκ ἔστιν αἰσθητῶν. οἱ γὰρ τὰ αἰσθητὰ νοσήματα θεραπεύοντες οὐ δύνανται πᾶσιν λέγειν· θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι; Ἰησοῦς δὲ καὶ τὸ θέλειν χαρίζεται, καὶ τὸ πιστεύειν λαμβάνει, καὶ τὴν δωρεὰν ἀμισθὶ χαρίζεται. 5 Περιῄει ποτὲ ὁ σωτὴρ κατὰ τὴν ὁδόν, καὶ τυφλοὶ δύο ἐκαθέζοντο, ἀβλεπτοῦντες μὲν τῷ σώματι, πεφωτισμένοι δὲ τὴν διάνοιαν. ὅνπερ γὰρ οὐκ ᾔδεισαν γραμματεῖς, τοῦτον ἐδείκνυον οἱ τυφλοὶ βοῶντες. οἱ μὲν γὰρ φαρισαῖοι τὸν νόμον μεμαθηκότες καὶ ἐκ παιδίου ἕως γήρως μεμελετηκότες καὶ ἐν ἀμαθίᾳ γεγηρακότες ἔλεγον, ὅτι τοῦτον οὐκ οἴδαμεν πόθεν ἐστίν. εἰς γὰρ τὰ ἴδια ἦλθεν, καὶ οἱ ἴδιοι αὐτὸν οὐ παρέλαβον. οἱ δὲ τυφλοὶ ἐπεβόων λέγοντες, υἱὲ ∆αβίδ, ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς. καὶ ὅνπερ οὐκ ᾔδεισαν οἱ τὸν νόμον μεμαθηκότες, τοῦτον ᾔδεισαν οἱ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς μὴ ὑπηρετήσαντας εἰς ἀνάγνωσιν ἔχοντες. Τούτοις προσελθὼν ὁ σωτὴρ ἔλεγεν· πιστεύετε ὅτι δύναμαι τοῦτο ποιῆσαι; καὶ τὸ τί θέλετε ἵνα ποιήσω ὑμῖν; οὐκ εἶπεν, τί θέλετε ἵνα εἴπω ὑμῖν, ἀλλά, τί θέλετε ἵνα ποιήσω ὑμῖν. ποιητὴς γὰρ ἦν καὶ ζωοδότης, οὐ νῦν ἀρξάμενος ποιεῖν. ὁ πατὴρ γὰρ αὐτοῦ πάντοτε ἐργάζεται, καὶ αὐτὸς τῷ πατρὶ συνεργάζεται, καὶ ποιητὴς ἦν τῶν ὅλων νεύματι πατρός. αὐτὸς δὲ μόνος ἐκ μόνου ἀμεσιτεύτως γεννηθεὶς ἐρωτᾷ τοὺς τυφλούς, λέγων· τί θέλετε ἵνα ποιήσω ὑμῖν;
orientation: Cyril opens his homily by declaring that wherever Jesus appears there is salvation, and he begins describing the pool of Bethesda and the paralytic who lay there thirty-eight years.
pass_a_gloss: Wherever Jesus appears, there also is salvation. For whether he sees a tax collector sitting at the tax booth, this one he makes an apostle and evangelist, or whether he is buried with the dead, he raises the dead. And to the blind he grants seeing, and to the deaf hearing. And he goes around the pools, not seeking the buildings, but healing the sick. For in Jerusalem there was a sheep pool having five porticoes, four running around, and the fifth in the middle, in which lay a multitude of the sick. And there was much unbelief of the Jews. But the physician and healer of souls and bodies granted the healing in measure, healing first the one of long duration, in order that he might be released more quickly from the pains. For it was not one day for him to lie there, nor a second, nor a first month or year, but thirty-eight years. Lying there with a long-lasting disease he was known to those who saw him, and showing the working of the one who heals. For the paralytic was recognized by all because of the time. But the great physician showed his power, yet was rejected by those who received him badly. Going around the pool he saw, not having learned from questioning, but from divine working he filled up what was lacking. Seeing, not asking, from how much time he lies there, but seeing he knew, the one who knew even before seeing. For if concerning the things in the heart he had no need that anyone should ask him about the man (for he himself knew what was in the man), much more concerning the diseases, of which the onset is from outside. He saw someone lying there and weighed down with a very great disease. For he had a heavy burden of sins and a long-lasting pain of disease. To this one he speaks a question somehow desired: Do you wish to become well? And he did not say anything else, but he left it to the middle ground of the question. For the question was double. For since not only was the body sick, but also the soul, (according to what was said later by him, See, you have become well, sin no more, lest something worse happen to you,) he asked him: Do you wish to become well? O of great power of a physician, who places the help upon the willing. For since salvation is from faith, for this reason he heard the Do you wish, in order that the willing might bring on the working. This is the word of Jesus alone. For it is not of physical physicians. For those who heal physical diseases cannot say to all: Do you wish to become well? But Jesus both grants the willing, and receives the believing, and grants the gift without pay. The savior once went along the road, and two blind men were sitting, blind in body, but enlightened in mind. For the one whom the scribes did not know, this one the blind men pointed out crying out. For the Pharisees, having learned the law and having studied from childhood to old age and having grown old in ignorance, said, We do not know where this one is from. For he came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But the blind men cried out saying, Son of David, have mercy on us. And the one whom those who had learned the law did not know, this one those who had eyes not serving for reading knew. To these the savior came near and said: Do you believe that I am able to do this? And the What do you wish that I should do for you? He did not say, What do you wish that I should say to you, but, What do you wish that I should do for you. For he was a maker and life-giver, not now beginning to make. For his father always works, and he himself works together with the father, and he was maker of all things by the nod of the father. But he alone, begotten from the only one without mediation, asks the blind men, saying: What do you wish that I should do for you?

pass_b_english: Wherever Jesus appears, there salvation is also. If he sees a tax collector sitting at the tax booth, he makes him an apostle and evangelist. If he is buried among the dead, he raises the dead. He grants sight to the blind and hearing to the deaf. He goes around the pools, not looking at the buildings but healing the sick.

For in Jerusalem there was a sheep pool with five porticoes: four running around it, and the fifth in the middle, where a crowd of the sick lay. And there was great unbelief among the Jews. But the physician and healer of souls and bodies granted healing in due measure, healing first the one who had suffered the longest, so that he might be released more quickly from his pains. For it was not one day that he lay there, nor a second, nor a first month or a year, but thirty-eight years. Lying there with his long illness, he was known to those who saw him, and he showed the working of the one who heals. For the paralytic was recognized by everyone because of the length of time. The great physician showed his power, but he was rejected by those who received him badly.

Going around the pool, he saw him. He did not learn from questioning, but from divine working he supplied what was lacking. Seeing, not asking, how long he had lain there, he saw and knew, the one who knew even before he saw. For if in matters of the heart he had no need for anyone to ask him about a person, for he himself knew what was in the person (John 2:25), how much more did he know about illnesses, whose onset comes from outside?

He saw a certain man lying there, weighed down by a very great illness. For he had a heavy burden of sins and the long-lasting pain of disease. To this man he speaks a question that was longed for: "Do you want to become well?" (John 5:6) He did not say anything else, but left it in the middle ground of the question. For the question was double. Since not only his body was sick but also his soul, according to what was said by him later: "See, you have become well; sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you" (John 5:14), he asked him: "Do you want to become well?" O the power of the great physician, who places help upon the willing! For since salvation comes from faith, he heard the "Do you want," so that the willing might bring about the working. This saying belongs to Jesus alone. It does not belong to physical physicians. For those who heal physical diseases cannot say to everyone: "Do you want to become well?" But Jesus grants even the willing, receives the believing, and gives the gift without payment.

Once the Savior was passing along the road, and two blind men were sitting there, blind in body but enlightened in mind. For the one whom the scribes did not know, the blind men pointed out by crying aloud. The Pharisees had learned the law and studied it from childhood to old age, and they had grown old in ignorance, saying: "We do not know where this man is from." For he came to his own, and his own did not receive him (John 1:11). But the blind men cried out, saying: "Son of David, have mercy on us." And the one whom those who had learned the law did not know, those who had eyes that did not serve them for reading knew. The Savior came to them and said: "Do you believe that I am able to do this?" And: "What do you want me to do for you?" (Matthew 20:32) He did not say, "What do you want me to say to you," but, "What do you want me to do for you." For he was a maker and life-giver, not now beginning to make. For his Father is always working (John 5:17), and he works together with the Father, and he was the maker of all things by the nod of the Father. He alone, begotten from the Father alone without mediation, asks the blind men, saying: "What do you want me to do for you?"

problems.why: Subject is Jesus, not the man; 'he heard' misattributes who heard. Jesus said 'Do you want' to summon willing into working.
problems.fix: for this reason he said, 'Do you want,' so that the willing might bring about the working
problems.ruling: Greek ἤκουσε τὸ θέλεις = Jesus heard the man's desire, not his own question 'Do you want', so translation misattributes subject.

fixed: Changed 'he heard' to 'he said' because the source's ἤκουσε refers to Jesus speaking the words 'Do you want,' not to the man hearing them; the subject is Jesus, who utters the question to summon the willing into action.
